verdict.reasoning: Patient first says symptoms have been over the past month and later specifies, when asked, that they started “probably a month and a half, maybe two months.”

Patient reports “losing feeling, in my hands and arms. I get a weird sensation like…pins and needles” and confirms it is the right hand; also states “I feel like my arm is getting weaker…for a few days and then goes back to normal,” indicating episodic paresthesias and weakness in the right upper limb.

Patient says “my colleague said, I'm walking slightly differently to normal” and later “at the same time I get my arm symptoms, my leg feels weaker,” indicating concurrent leg weakness with gait change noted by a colleague.
Patient reports “recently I've noticed, I can't hold my cup of coffee. And when I do drink coffee, it's slightly harder to drink…Only during the episodes.”
When asked about difficulty swallowing during episodes, patient says “I, I, I feel like there's something in my throat,” matching the sensation of ‘something there’ in the throat during episodes.
Patient states “I generally feel tired, and weak. And, sometimes I feel nauseous,” which corresponds to fatigue, generalized weakness, and occasional nausea.
Patient describes frequency: “at the start, it would be maybe once a week, uh, to every once, once a month, but now it's getting uh, uh, a couple of times a day.”
Patient notes “it only lasts few days and then goes back to normal,” indicating episodes of variable duration lasting a few days then resolving.

When asked about speaking: “What about…difficulty speaking during these episodes? Any issues with that at all?” Patient replies “No, I can speak fine.” For vision: “And any visual problems during these episodes?” Patient: “I, I don't think so, but I wear glasses.” This supports denial of dysarthria and visual changes during episodes.
Doctor asks “Do you have the symptoms right now?” and patient replies “No, I'm perfectly fine at the moment,” indicating no current symptoms.

When asked about other illnesses, patient answers “No.” Earlier, regarding self, patient says no history of mini-strokes: “Have you had any history of, mini-strokes…?” Patient: “No…” Thus no past medical history mentioned and no prior TIA/CVA.
Patient states “I take an aspirin, seventy five milligrams, once a day, but that's, because of something I read on the internet,” confirming self-initiated Aspirin 75 mg daily.
In response to allergies, patient says “I'm allergic to penicillin only.”
Patient reports “my father has had a, operation to the side of his neck, to reduce the risk of stroke,” consistent with carotid surgery to reduce stroke risk.
Patient says “I'm, uh, I'm actually a doctor… I work in, uh, plastic surgery” and later “No, I live with my wife,” matching a plastic surgery doctor living with his wife.
When asked “do you smoke at all?” patient replies “No, I don't,” indicating non-smoker status.

Symptoms described are transient focal neurological (right hand/arm weakness, leg weakness, abnormal gait, throat sensation). Doctor explicitly states “They make me concerned about, mini-strokes or TIAs, transient ischemic attacks…our presumptive, working diagnosis is, mini-stroke or TIA,” supporting concern for TIA.

Patient explains Aspirin use is “because of something I read on the internet” and confirms no GP discussion of its risks or indication: “Has any GP ever spoken to you about, the risks of Aspirin…?…Patient: No, I haven't,” confirming use without medical recommendation.

Doctor says “I'm going to, refer you to a stroke, a TIA clinic… I send that referral off now, and then you can attend them, they, they'll usually, call you in within the next one to two days…today it's Wednesday…deadline should be, Thursday, Friday,” confirming urgent referral with 1–2 day target.

Doctor notes “they'll be doing a ultrasound of the, carotid arteries, like your, your father had. Um, and, they'll be doing a, maybe a, they might do a scan of your brain as well,” indicating anticipated carotid Doppler and possible brain imaging.

Doctor says “The hospital, you can actually ring them, on um, uh, the PALS number, and then there's also the TIA clinic number. I'm going to leave that number in the notes…If you want, you can ring them, either today or tomorrow morning…just to find out when they got time to slot you in,” matching provision of contact numbers and advice to call today or tomorrow.

Doctor advises “If your symptoms return and they persist, they're prolonged. Then um, you may need to attend A and E…if a mini-stroke is prolonged then…that becomes even more of an emergency…we want you to go to hospital in that instance, as soon as possible,” consistent with safety-net to attend A&E immediately if prolonged/persistent.

Doctor states “if there's any delay that, transpires for example, you can't make the appointment or, you know, they, you don't get called…you get, get in contact back, back with us,” advising to contact the practice if unable to attend or delays occur.
